measurement.happened:
This week in Turkey was dominated by three major storylines that together painted a picture of a country under industrial, financial, and diplomatic pressure.

The most visceral event was the deadly explosion at a steel plant in western Turkey (Izmir area), which killed between 16 and 18 workers depending on the source and left 13 injured. Reuters, BBC, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, AFP, and Deutsche Welle all covered the blast. In the days that followed, workers demanded answers, families grieved, and the anger spread. AFP reported at least nine people detained while protesting at the blast site, and by November 14 the death toll was still being confirmed at 17 or 18. Bloomberg noted the plant belonged to a top Turkish steel exporter, which means the disaster has trade and export implications. The local community is also dealing with a longer-running grievance: residents of Adana have been refusing to be 'Europe's plastic dump,' a complaint that TV5Monde and BBC both picked up, suggesting the steel blast is part of a broader pattern of industrial neglect in Turkey's western and southern provinces.

The second major story is the banking and fund scandal that is engulfing Turkey's financial regulators. The chairman of Turkey's banking watchdog submitted his resignation directly to Erdogan (Reuters, FT). Bloomberg reported that the ex-CEO of Takasbank (the central securities depository) was arrested in what is being called a widening fund crackdown, and that the scandal involves roughly $20 billion in fraudulent or mismanaged funds. The FT framed it as the 'chief banking regulator offering to resign over a $20bn fraud scandal.' Bloomberg also noted that Turkey raised its inflation forecasts partly due to the 'fund-rout effects' of the scandal. A global crypto watchdog separately urged Turkey to strengthen its crypto rules, suggesting the financial sector is under multiple pressures at once.

The third major thread is Turkey's role as host of COP31, the UN climate summit, which ran from November 9 through roughly November 14. Erdogan used the podium to call the war in Gaza an 'ecocide' (AP), pushed a zero-waste plan, and declared that Turkey's climate goals will cost roughly $300 billion (Bloomberg). Istanbul alone faces a $100 billion green-transition bill. The summit also produced a record $1.6 billion climate-policy deal between Turkey and the AIIB. Meanwhile, Deutsche Welle noted the irony of Turkey pushing a coal-to-clean transition while its beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles, and farmers are being hit by extreme weather. The summit was a stage for Turkey to project multilateral leadership.

On the energy and trade front, a flurry of deals was signed or advanced: China signed a preliminary $15 billion deal for solar and wind power plants in Turkey (Reuters); Saudi Arabia and Turkey agreed to build 3,000 MW of wind capacity (Reuters); Canada's AtkinsRealis signed a deal for a feasibility study on a possible nuclear plant (Reuters, FT, Bloomberg); and Turkey is reportedly nearing a final nuclear power deal, with Canada and South Korea as the favored candidates (Bloomberg). These deals signal that Turkey is aggressively diversifying its energy imports and trying to become a regional energy hub.

On the defense and security side, Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement pledging a unified stance against any attack (Reuters). A military helicopter crashed in eastern/southern Turkey, killing four service members (Reuters, AP). Deutsche Welle reported that Turkey is using espionage accusations as a pressure tactic against government critics, a pattern that has intensified in recent weeks.

In domestic politics, TV5Monde (in French) reported that seven detained mayors have joined Turkey's main opposition party, signaling a consolidation of local opposition figures around a single banner after their releases or while still in custody. Erdogan publicly condemned protests over a rival's arrest as a 'movement of violence' (DW). The espionage-accusation thread (DW, two separate articles) suggests Ankara is using intelligence-service allegations to sideline or intimidate political opponents and journalists.

In sports, Turkey played Belgium in the UEFA Nations League on November 12 and faces France on November 14, so the national football team is in a competitive window. A minor but colorful story: the yacht captain from the reality show 'Below Deck' was arrested in Turkey after a teenager died (AP), adding a splash of international celebrity to the week's news cycle.

In summary, this week combined a deadly industrial disaster with public anger, a major financial-sector scandal shaking the banking regulator, a high-profile climate summit where Turkey tried to punch above its weight, a series of significant energy and defense deals, and ongoing political maneuvering involving the opposition, espionage accusations, and Erdogan's rhetorical management of all of it.
measurement.expected:
Looking ahead to the week of November 14 through roughly November 21, 2026, here is my theme-by-theme read.

Steel plant aftermath and worker unrest: It is almost certain that the investigation into the Izmir steel plant blast will continue to dominate domestic headlines. Expect the government to announce an official inquiry, possibly name a commission, and promise compensation packages for the families of the dead. It is probable that further arrests of plant managers or safety officials will follow the initial nine detained protesters, and that Erdogan will either visit the site or address the nation to project control. There is a possible, though not certain, risk of a second wave of strikes or sit-downs at other steel or metal plants if the compensation or safety findings are seen as inadequate. I would rate a full-blown general industrial strike as unlikely but not impossible. The Adana 'plastic dump' grievance may get a government response or a new waste-management announcement, but a major policy shift within one week is unlikely.

Banking and fund scandal: The resignation of the banking watchdog chairman is already submitted, so in the coming days it is almost certain that Erdogan will either formally accept it and announce a successor, or negotiate a quiet exit. The appointment of a new BDDK (banking regulator) head will be a closely watched political signal. It is probable that one or two more arrests or indictments will follow in the Takasbank / $20bn fund case, as the 'widening crackdown' language in Bloomberg suggests the net is still being cast. Markets will likely remain jumpy; expect the lira to feel pressure if the successor is seen as less independent. A full-blown bank run is possible but I would rate it as a moderate tail risk rather than the base case. The crypto-asset rule push from the global watchdog will probably result in a Turkish regulatory body issuing a statement or a draft rule within the week, but a major new law is unlikely this fast.

COP31 follow-through and energy deals: The summit itself is wrapping up, so it is almost certain that Turkey will issue a final communiqué or ministerial declaration in the next day or two. The $1.6bn AIIB climate deal and the $300bn climate-cost figure will be cited in follow-up press releases. The China $15bn solar/wind preliminary deal, the Saudi 3,000MW wind agreement, and the Canada nuclear feasibility study are all at different stages of maturity. I would expect at least one of these to move to a more concrete implementation or financing announcement within the week, but a full contract signing for the nuclear plant is unlikely before year-end. The $100bn Istanbul green-transition bill will generate local political debate, possibly with opposition mayors using it as a budget argument.

Defense and security: The Turkey-Qatar mutual defence pact will generate follow-up commentary from both governments and from regional observers (Greece, Egypt, Israel). I would expect a joint statement or a small-scale coordination meeting within the week, but no dramatic operational deployment. The helicopter crash investigation will be ongoing; a preliminary cause report is possible but a full findings document is unlikely within seven days. The espionage-accusation thread is the one to watch: it is probable that at least one more prominent critic (a journalist, an academic, or a local politician) will be named or questioned, keeping the DW-style 'pressure tactic' narrative alive. A full-scale arrest wave is possible but not the most likely outcome.

Opposition and domestic politics: With seven detained mayors now in the main opposition party, it is almost certain that the opposition will hold a press conference or a small rally to present a unified front and to demand a parliamentary debate on the steel-plant safety record and the banking scandal. Erdogan's 'movement of violence' rhetoric suggests he will keep the opposition on the back foot with a speech or a social-media post. A surprise cabinet reshuffle is possible but I would rate it as less likely than a targeted swap of two or three ministers (possibly the energy or finance minister) to signal control after the banking scandal.

Sports: Turkey plays France in the UEFA Nations League on November 14 (or in the next couple of days). The result will be a major domestic conversation, either a victory celebration or a post-match analysis of what went wrong. This is a near-certain headline, though its political weight is modest.

Less-likely surprises (possible but I would not build my forecast around them): a second industrial accident at another plant within the same week; a sudden lira devaluation of more than 5 percent triggered by the banking news; a surprise Erdogan-Qatar joint military exercise announcement; a major earthquake in a seismically active region (always a background risk in Turkey); the Below Deck yacht-captain case becoming a diplomatic footnote if the teenager's family hails from a G20 country.

Things I would not bet on: a snap parliamentary election being called within this week; a full military confrontation or border incident with Greece or Syria; a government collapse or no-confidence vote; a new nuclear test or missile launch; a major currency crisis where the lira loses more than 15 percent in a single day; a constitutional referendum being announced; or a complete shutdown of the Istanbul stock exchange.

Overall, the next week will be a mix of managing the steel-plant fallout, navigating the banking scandal's political and market consequences, converting COP31 momentum into concrete energy deals, and Erdogan's ongoing rhetorical and institutional management of the opposition and the media. It is a busy, multi-threaded week but not one where a single black-swan event is the most likely outcome.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs five days apart, several themes grew noticeably while others faded or were replaced. The steel plant explosion in Izmir went from a breaking-news event (16 dead, 4 missing, Erdogan promising to find the truth) to a settled but still-angry story: the death toll was confirmed at 17 or 18, thirteen workers were injured, nine people were detained while protesting at the blast site, and the narrative broadened to include the Adana community's long-running complaint about being 'Europe's plastic dump,' linking the steel disaster to a wider pattern of industrial neglect in Turkey's western and southern provinces. The fund scandal widened in both scope and seniority: in the first photo the arrests hit the stock exchange CEO, the clearinghouse CEO, and a former minister; by the second photo the chairman of Turkey's banking watchdog had submitted his resignation directly to Erdogan, the ex-CEO of Takasbank was arrested, the $20 billion figure was confirmed in mainstream reporting, and the central bank raised its inflation forecasts partly because of the 'fund-rout effects.' COP31 moved from a launch-and-preparation story to a summit in its final days, producing concrete deals: a $1.6 billion climate-policy agreement with the AIIB, a preliminary $15 billion Chinese solar-and-wind package, a 3,000-megawatt Saudi wind deal, and a Canadian nuclear feasibility study. Erdogan's $500 billion electrification plan was restated as roughly $300 billion, and he used the podium to call the Gaza war an 'ecocide,' a political overlay the first photo had not yet shown. Defense diplomacy shifted: the Saudi-Pakistan pact and the Azerbaijan thaw that dominated the first photo gave way to a new Turkey-Qatar mutual defense agreement and a military helicopter crash that killed four service members. The media-and-opposition thread evolved from street protests over journalist arrests to a more structural realignment: seven detained mayors joined the main opposition party, Erdogan labeled rival protests a 'movement of violence,' and Deutsche Welle reported two separate stories about Ankara using espionage accusations as a systematic pressure tactic against critics. New items that appeared only in the second photo include the crypto watchdog urging stronger Turkish rules, the Below Deck yacht-captain arrest, and the DW piece on beaches becoming too hot for sea turtles. Items that shrank or vanished include the Togg EV uncertainty, the US sanctions on Turkish firms for aiding Iran, the Turkish Cypriot gas pipeline, the Erdogan-Putin-Zelenskiy triangle, the Ocalan prison move, the Amedspor football story, and the one-off cultural pieces about Viking graffiti and the 'Turkish Maldives.' The Fenerbahce-Liverpool match and the rural western-Turkey shootings also dropped out of the frame, as expected for single-event stories.
delta.wind: COP31 negotiations were rated almost certain, and they came true, though in a slightly different shape than predicted. The expectation was for bilateral deals around the gas pipeline or the 500-billion-dollar plan, and instead the deals that materialized were the AIIB climate package, the Chinese solar-and-wind contract, the Saudi wind agreement, and the Canadian nuclear study. The 'don't mention coal' strategy was tested exactly as foreseen, with DW highlighting the irony of a coal-to-clean pitch while sea turtles suffer on overheated beaches. A surprise was Erdogan's 'ecocide' remark on Gaza, which turned a climate summit into a broader geopolitical stage. The fund scandal was rated probable for further arrests and market jitters, and it came true and then exceeded expectations: the resignation of the top banking regulator to Erdogan is a bigger political event than 'one or two more detentions,' and the link to inflation forecasts shows the macroeconomic bleed-through that was only hinted at. The parliamentary flashpoint did not clearly materialize as a formal question, but the resignation itself is a political act. The steel plant aftermath was rated probable, and it hit: workers protested, nine were detained, and the Adana plastic-dump story broadened the industrial-safety narrative beyond a single blast. The expectation of a small workers' demonstration was met and then slightly exceeded by the detentions. Turkey-Azerbaijan and defense diplomacy were rated possible, and the outcome was a partial miss in the specific form predicted: the Azerbaijan thaw and the US-sanctions response were not prominent in the second photo, while the Turkey-Qatar defense pact and the helicopter crash were not on the list at all. The Erdogan-Putin-Zelenskiy phone call or statement did not appear. Media protests were rated possible for a follow-up demonstration, and the reality was more structural: the seven mayors joining the opposition and the espionage-accusation pattern represent a deeper political realignment than a second street march, though Erdogan's 'movement of violence' remark shows the street tension is still live. Inflation and monetary policy were rated possible, and they came true through the fund-rout channel rather than as a standalone central-bank decision. The things the expectation said it would not bet on (cabinet reshuffle, border incident, central-bank governor change, constitutional referendum, trade-bloc shift) did not appear, which is consistent. The main pattern of error is that the expectation underestimated the speed at which the fund scandal would climb the regulatory hierarchy, over-weighted the Azerbaijan and US-sanctions threads, and did not anticipate the concrete energy deals (China, Saudi, Canada) that COP31 produced. It also did not foresee the espionage-accusation mechanism or the mayors' opposition consolidation, both of which point to a more systematic political tightening than the protest cycle alone would suggest.
delta.driver: The force pushing Turkey from the first photograph to the second is the tension between an outward projection of rising-power status and the internal costs of sustaining that projection. COP31 gave Erdogan a global stage and a deadline, and the government used the five-day window to lock in energy deals with China, Saudi Arabia, Canada, and the AIIB while signing a new defense pact with Qatar, all of which reinforce the narrative that Turkey is a regional hub and a multilateral player. But the same growth-at-speed model that produces steel plants, fund-driven market activity, and rapid infrastructure buildout is also producing the Izmir explosion, the $20 billion fund fraud, and the banking regulator's resignation. The financial scandal is not just a corruption story; it is a macroeconomic one that is already feeding into inflation forecasts and lira pressure, which in turn constrains the government's ability to fund the $300 billion green-transition bill it is selling at the summit. Domestically, the opposition is consolidating (mayors joining a single banner) while the government responds with espionage accusations, media pressure, and rhetorical framing of dissent as 'violence,' suggesting a leadership that is simultaneously reaching outward for deals and tightening inward for control. The driver, in short, is a government racing to cement Turkey's new geopolitical position before the internal financial and industrial cracks become too expensive to hide, using the COP31 window as both a deal-making opportunity and a distraction from a widening domestic crisis.

The motion is clearly upward and the scope is widening from the financial sector into political territory. The resignation is a political act: Erdogan must either accept it (signaling the scandal is serious enough to cost a top official) or reject it (signaling control). Either way, it generates a parliamentary question, media firestorm, and likely one or two more arrests in the coming days. The inflation-forecast link means the central bank is now in the story too, and the lira will remain under pressure. I have been consistently underestimating the speed of this escalation, so I should expect at least one more senior figure to be hit and a formal parliamentary or committee event.

The steel explosion is moving from shock to institutionalized grievance. The nine detentions at the blast site, the Adana plastic-dump story, and the broader western/southern industrial-neglect pattern suggest the opposition will use this in parliament and the workers will organize a second wave. The motion is from a single event to a sector-wide safety review. I should not expect a second explosion, but I should expect the theme to persist through parliamentary questions, a government commission, and continued street-level anger.

COP31 is over. My track record says signed agreements go quiet within a week—the Canada strategic partnership was the biggest deal of early November and it barely registered by the following week. So the $15bn China deal, the Saudi wind pact, and the AIIB package will be in the background. However, the nuclear-deal shortlist (Canada vs South Korea) might produce a technical announcement, and the $300bn green-transition cost will be a talking point as the government tries to fund it. I should expect a joint opposition statement, a parliamentary question linking the fund scandal to the steel explosion, and possibly another espionage accusation against a journalist or local politician. My track record says I underestimate the street and the opposition's structural moves, so I should weight this higher.

The energy and defense deals are in implementation mode. The Turkey-Qatar pact was just signed and will go quiet. The helicopter crash is a one-off. The crypto-regulation story might produce a specific rule or consultation. The France match on Nov 14 is a single event.

Correcting for the wind: I have been wrong in three consistent ways. First, I underestimate the speed at which institutional problems escalate into arrests and top-level resignations. So for the fund scandal, I should expect the escalation to continue at least one more step. Second, I overestimate the headline-generating power of signed diplomatic agreements. So the COP31 deals and the Qatar pact should be lower-confidence as front-page stories. Third, I underestimate the street and the opposition's structural moves. So the mayors' consolidation and the espionage-accusation pattern should be weighted higher than a simple 'another protest' forecast. I also keep missing new diplomatic initiatives that are not in the visible pipeline, so I should allow for one unexpected diplomatic development.

What I would not bet on: a cabinet reshuffle beyond the banking watchdog resignation, a border incident with Greece or Syria, a central-bank governor change (that's a different position from the banking watchdog), a constitutional referendum, a second major industrial disaster in the same week, a full lira crash over 10%, a military clash, or an earthquake. These are all possible but the motion does not point toward them, and my track record says the 'not bet on' list has held in most rounds.

emoji_reasons: The $20 billion banking-fund scandal has just reached the top of the regulatory hierarchy with the banking watchdog chairman's resignation, and the motion points to further arrests and parliamentary action.

The Izmir steel-plant explosion that killed 17 or 18 workers is shifting from a single disaster to a sector-wide industrial-safety story, with protests, detentions, and a broader grievance about Turkey's western and southern industry.

crystal.tldr: Turkey's $20 billion banking-fund scandal is about to hit the political stratosphere, with the banking watchdog chairman's resignation to Erdogan likely triggering a parliamentary firestorm and at least one more arrest. The Izmir steel-plant explosion is broadening into a sector-wide industrial-safety crisis, with worker protests and opposition questions linking it to the government's growth-at-all-costs model. crystal.eli5:
Turkey is having a really rough week, and next week is likely to be rougher. Imagine a big bank where the person in charge of checking that everything is honest just walked in and said, "I quit, the boss, because I found $20 billion missing." That's basically what happened. The person who quit is the head of the banking watchdog, and the boss is President Erdogan. Next week, the parliament is going to want answers, more people are likely to get arrested, and the Turkish lira (the money) is going to keep wobbling because people are nervous about their savings.

On top of that, a steel factory in the city of Izmir exploded and killed about 17 or 18 workers. The families and other workers are angry, and the government caught some of them in the act of protesting and locked them up. Now the story is spreading to other cities where factories are bad and the air is dirty and nobody seems to care. The opposition politicians are going to use this to say, "See? You're building too fast and not checking the safety." The government is going to say, "We'll set up a committee to look into it," which is the political equivalent of saying, "We'll get back to you."

And underneath all of this, the opposition parties are getting more organized. Seven mayors who had been arrested or detained have all joined the same opposition party, which is like a group of rival coaches all signing with the same team. At the same time, the government has been accusing journalists and critics of being spies for foreign countries, which is a way of saying, "You're not just criticizing us; you're working for the enemy." So next week, you can expect the opposition to get louder and more united, the government to get more aggressive with its accusations, and the banking scandal to keep throwing up new names. It's going to be a loud week in Ankara.
